Reproducing Doherty et al. (2025) from dandiset 001444¶

Paper. Doherty DW, Chen L, Smith Y, Wichmann T, Chu H-Y, Lytton WW (2025). Enhanced beta power emerges from simulated parkinsonian primary motor cortex. npj Parkinson's Disease 11, 230. doi:10.1038/s41531-025-01070-4.

Claims. claims/001444/10.1038-s41531-025-01070-4.yaml, written from the version of record (Europe PMC, PMC12325672: main text, legends and Methods; the supplement was not available) and checked by a second reader. The claims file decides what is tested and how.

Dandiset. DANDI:001444, version 0.250805.2002. The paper's data statement names the dandiset without a version. This is the only published version, and the draft holds the same 17 assets with the same blobs (data check), so the pinned version holds what the paper deposited.

What the dandiset holds. Four sets of four NetPyNE simulations of a 10,073-cell model of mouse M1, 4.3 s each: control and parkinsonian, rest and activated, per set. The paper's results come from set sM1_12-12-2023 (Methods, paragraph 2), files sub-001_ses-sM1-12-12-2023-01 to -04. Each file holds spike times of the cells that fired, one LFP trace and somatic potentials of 20 (paper's set) or 400 (other sets) PT5B cells. One asset, sub-001/sub-001.nwb, is a second copy of sub-001_ses-sM1-04-22-2024-01.nwb.

Outside inputs. None. The spectrogram of reading S1 is a copy of NetPyNE 1.0.5's Morlet method in the helper; it is software the Methods name, not data.

loaded 16 files of dandiset 001444 version 0.250805.2002 in 171 s

Data check¶

Each check of the description against the values is stated under its output. The archive's description of the dandiset says each file holds "a local field potential trace, spike train data from all 10,073 neurons, and membrane potential traces from 400 of the layer 5B pyramidal tract (PT5B) neurons", and that simulations last 4.3 s.

The version holds 17 assets: four sets of four simulations, named by set and number, and sub-001/sub-001.nwb, which is the same blob as sub-001_ses-sM1-04-22-2024-01.nwb (a recording deposited twice; it is counted once and not read again). The archive lists no related resource, and its summary gives "spike sorting technique" as the measurement technique of a simulation.

Expected order of the numbered files (claims file):  {'01': 'control rest', '02': 'parkinsonian rest', '03': 'control activated', '04': 'parkinsonian activated'}

The session descriptions confirm the numbering of the claims file: -01 control rest ("quiet wakefulness"), -02 parkinsonian rest, -03 control activated ("movement"), -04 parkinsonian activated, in every set. Spike times run from 0 to 4.3 s and are in seconds; no unit has zero spikes, and every train is sorted. The LFP has 172,000 samples at 40 kHz, 4.3 s. The files of the paper's set (sM1-12-12-2023) hold 20 PT5B membrane potentials, not 400 as the description says; the other sets hold 400. Each file holds one LFP trace, "LFP 0", where the model records 11 electrodes (claims file, cfg.recordLFP); no file says at which depth it was taken.

The units table holds only cells that fired: 2,917 to 4,480 M1 units per file of the paper's set, not 10,073, and input generators that did not fire are missing too (fewer than 1,000 per input region). The cell names carry NetPyNE's gids, numbered in one block per population; the inputs start at gid 10073, so the M1 cells are gids 0 to 10072, which is consistent with 10,073 cells. The size of each population is bounded from the gids seen in any of the 16 files; for the populations the claims use the bounds differ by at most 8 cells (IT6; IT2, IT4 and IT5A by 1), and the rates under both bounds are shown below. PT5B has 1,435 cells and all fired in every file.

# Clock and labels: upward 0 mV crossings of each membrane potential trace against the spike
# times of the unit with the same gid: the share of unit spikes with a crossing within 0.5 ms, by
# span of time. The paper's set (20 traces per file) and, for comparison, the first 20 traces of
# each file of set sM1-04-22-2024.
rows = []
for c, d in D.items():
    for r in m.vm_match(d["vm"], d["trains"]):
        rows.append({"set": m.PAPER_SET, "file": c, "pop": d["pop"].get(r["gid"]), **r,
                     "Vm min": d["vm"][r["gid"]].min(), "Vm max": d["vm"][r["gid"]].max()})
VM_OTHER = {c: m.load_vm_subset("sM1-04-22-2024", c, 20) for c in m.CONDITIONS}
for c, vmd in VM_OTHER.items():
    d = OTHER[("sM1-04-22-2024", c)]
    for r in m.vm_match(vmd, d["trains"]):
        rows.append({"set": "sM1-04-22-2024", "file": c, "pop": d["pop"].get(r["gid"]), **r,
                     "Vm min": vmd[r["gid"]].min(), "Vm max": vmd[r["gid"]].max()})
vmchk = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(vmchk.groupby(["set", "file"]).agg(traces=("gid", "size"), all_PT5B=("pop", lambda s: bool((s == "PT5B").all())),
      Vm_spikes=("Vm spikes", "sum"), unit_spikes=("unit spikes", "sum"),
      matched_0_05s=("0-0.5 s", "mean"), matched_05_2s=("0.5-2.0 s", "mean"), matched_2_43s=("2.0-4.3 s", "mean"),
      vm_min=("Vm min", "min"), vm_max=("Vm max", "max")).round(3).to_string())

Every trace belongs to a PT5B unit of the same gid. In set sM1-04-22-2024 the trace's 0 mV crossings fall on that unit's spike times throughout the 4.3 s, so there the potentials and the spikes share one clock and one labelling. In the paper's set they do only at the start: the crossings match the unit's spikes in the first 0.5 s, less from 0.5 to 2 s, and hardly at all in W (shares printed above), while the numbers of spikes stay similar. The potentials of the paper's set therefore come from a run that diverged from the one whose spikes are stored, with the same cells and the same start; that cannot be established from the files and is recorded as a finding. The potentials range over the values printed, in mV.

In [6]:
# LFP against the PT5B spike count histogram: the Results say the LFP and the PT5B SCH oscillate in
# antiphase. Correlation at lags from -50 to 50 ms (2 ms bins) in W; a shared clock puts the
# extreme near lag 0, and the contrast between rest (beta) and activated (gamma) shows in the lag
# of the next opposite extreme.
lags = np.arange(-25, 26)
rows = []
for c, d in D.items():
    _, cnt = m.sch(m.pop_spikes(d, "PT5B"))
    x = d["lfp"][int(m.WINDOW[0] * m.FS):int(m.WINDOW[1] * m.FS)]
    lfp2 = x[: len(cnt) * 80].reshape(len(cnt), 80).mean(axis=1)
    a, b = (cnt - cnt.mean()) / cnt.std(), (lfp2 - lfp2.mean()) / lfp2.std()
    r = np.array([np.mean(a[max(0, -k):len(a) - max(0, k)] * b[max(0, k):len(b) - max(0, -k)]) for k in lags])
    i = np.argmin(r)
    rows.append({"file": m.CONDITIONS[c], "r at lag 0": r[25], "most negative r": r[i], "its lag ms": lags[i] * 2,
                 "most positive r": r.max(), "its lag ms ": lags[np.argmax(r)] * 2})
    # shifted control: LFP shifted by 1 s
    sh = np.roll(b, 500)
    rows[-1]["r at lag 0, LFP shifted 1 s"] = np.mean(a * sh)
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))

In every file the LFP and the PT5B SCH are most strongly anticorrelated at a lag of a few ms, and the correlation is near zero when the LFP is shifted by 1 s, consistent with the antiphase the Results describe and with one clock for the LFP and the spikes in W.

The LFP and every potential series start at 0 s and are sampled at 40 kHz, so slicing at sample 2.0 s x 40 kHz takes W. "LFP 0" has no electrode, position or depth in any attribute, and the files have no extracellular electrodes table, so which of the 11 electrodes it is cannot be told (it is taken as electrode 0, reading E1, as before). The units table has only the name, segment, block, spike times and observation intervals of each unit, and no row for a cell that did not fire, so the silent cells cannot be listed from the files; R1 and the fig1 count rest on the gid blocks.

In [8]:
EXP = {}   # expected values of each claim, from the claims file, as (value, tolerance)

def within(x, e):
    return abs(x - e[0]) <= e[1] + 1e-9

def rate_rows(pop, conds):
    """Mean, sd and n of a population's rates in W under R1 (largest and smallest block), R2 and R3."""
    rows = []
    for c in conds:
        r = m.rates(D[c], pop, BLOCKS)
        rmin = m.rates(D[c], pop, BLOCKS, size="min")
        for name, x in [("R1", r["R1"]), ("R1 (smallest block)", rmin["R1"]), ("R2", r["R1"][r["R2_mask"]]),
                        ("R3", r["R1"][r["R3_mask"]])]:
            mu, sd, n = m.summary(x)
            rows.append({"file": c, "condition": m.CONDITIONS[c], "pop": pop, "reading": name,
                         "mean": mu, "sd": sd, "n": n})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def compare(pop, c1, c2):
    """p-values of T1 to T4 for rates of `pop` in files c1 and c2, under R1, R2 and R3. Cells are paired
    by gid (same network in all four files of a set). Under R2 and R3 the unpaired tests use the cells
    kept in each file, and the paired tests are run with two pairings: the cells kept in both files
    (rows "R2", "R3"), and the cells kept in either, at 0 in the file where they are not kept (rows
    "R2 union", "R3 union", whose unpaired tests are those of R2 and R3)."""
    a, b = m.rates(D[c1], pop, BLOCKS), m.rates(D[c2], pop, BLOCKS)
    out = []
    for name, ka, kb in [("R1", np.ones(len(a["R1"]), bool), np.ones(len(b["R1"]), bool)),
                         ("R2", a["R2_mask"], b["R2_mask"]), ("R3", a["R3_mask"], b["R3_mask"])]:
        both = ka & kb
        row = {"reading": name, "mean 1": a["R1"][ka].mean() if ka.any() else np.nan,
               "mean 2": b["R1"][kb].mean() if kb.any() else np.nan, "n paired": int(both.sum())}
        if both.sum() > 1:
            p = m.tests(a["R1"][both], b["R1"][both])
            row.update({k: p[k] for k in ["T1 Wilcoxon", "T2 paired t"]})
        if ka.sum() > 1 and kb.sum() > 1:
            p = m.tests(a["R1"][ka], b["R1"][kb], paired_ok=False)
            row.update(p)
        out.append(row)
        if name != "R1":
            either = ka | kb
            urow = dict(row, reading=name + " union", **{"n paired": int(either.sum())})
            if either.sum() > 1:
                p = m.tests(a["R1"][either], b["R1"][either])
                urow.update({k: p[k] for k in ["T1 Wilcoxon", "T2 paired t"]})
            out.append(urow)
    return pd.DataFrame(out)

def check_rates(cid, pop, conds, keys, stat=("mean", "sd")):
    t = rate_rows(pop, conds)
    print(t.round(3).to_string(index=False))
    print()
    for reading in ["R1", "R1 (smallest block)", "R2", "R3"]:
        sub = t[t.reading == reading].set_index("file")
        vals, ok = [], []
        for (c, s), e in zip(keys, EXP[cid]):
            v = sub.loc[c, s]
            vals.append(round(float(v), 3))
            ok.append(bool(within(v, e)) if np.isfinite(v) else False)
        print(f"{reading:22s} values {vals}  expected {[e[0] for e in EXP[cid]]}  within tolerance {ok}  all: {all(ok)}")

Claims¶

Rates are spikes in W (2.0 to 4.3 s) over 2.3 s. The claims file's rate readings are R1 (all cells of the population, silent ones at 0), R2 (cells with a spike in W) and R3 (cells with a spike in the 4.3 s simulation, those silent in W at 0). R3 was added to the claims file in answer to a question (questions/001444.yaml); since the files hold exactly the cells that fired, R3 is the cells the file holds. The paper does not say which cells enter a mean, so an outcome that holds only under R3 rests on that reading as an assumption. Test readings T1 to T4 are two-sided. Under R2 and R3 the paired tests are run with two pairings, since the claims file does not say which: the cells kept in both files, and the cells kept in either file with 0 where a cell is not kept ("union" rows). The first keeps every paired value inside the group whose mean is reported; the second adds, for each file, cells outside its group at 0 spikes/s. Where the two give different outcomes, the cells kept in both files are adopted, for that reason, and the outcome is marked as assumed.

fig1-network-size¶

The simulated M1 network is composed of 10,073 neurons of seven excitatory pyramidal cell types (IT, PT5B, CT) and two interneuron cell types (PV, SOM).

Criterion: count the units of the 15 M1 populations in each file of set sM1_12-12-2023; reproduced when the count is 10,073 in each.

Result: blocked (data_missing). The files of set sM1_12-12-2023 hold 4,480, 3,231, 2,919 and 2,917 M1 units, not 10,073, because only cells that fired are stored: no stored M1 unit is silent, and 5,593 to 7,156 of the gids 0 to 10072 have no row (printed above). The gids are consistent with the paper: the input generators start at gid 10073, all 15 M1 populations are present, and the gid blocks of the data check support 10,073 cells. The units table has no row or column for a cell that did not fire (data check), so the silent cells the criterion counts are not in the dataset, and the claim cannot be tested from these files. The data do not contradict the paper's 10,073. The outcome was not reproduced until the third verification round, which agreed with the change to blocked.

model-pt5b-excitability-decrease (blocked)¶

In the parkinsonian condition the PT5B neuron model was changed (BK and NaT conductances) so that its spike count across current injections fell by 64%, as in 6-OHDA mouse slices.

The dandiset holds only the 16 network simulations (data check); there are no single-cell current-injection simulations, so the claim is not tested.

robustness-four-sets (blocked, measures reported)¶

The results hold across four sets of four simulations with different random seeds; set sM1_12-12-2023 is a typical example and the other three sets are analysed in Supplementary Table 2.

The claims file gives no measures or values for this claim (Supplementary Table 2 was not available), so it is blocked. As the criterion allows, the measures of the claims below are reported for each set, without an outcome.

Dominant frequencies: fig2-control-rest-beta, fig2-control-activated-gamma, fig5-pd-rest-beta, fig5-pd-activated-gamma¶

fig2-control-rest-beta: In the control condition at rest, M1 activity is dominated by beta-band activity of about 20 Hz, particularly clear in the PT5B spike count histogram.

fig2-control-activated-gamma: In the control condition, the activated state shifts M1 activity to gamma-band activity of about 44 Hz.

fig5-pd-rest-beta: In the parkinsonian condition at rest, M1 activity shows focused beta-band activity at 15 Hz.

fig5-pd-activated-gamma: In the parkinsonian condition the activated state shifts M1 activity to gamma-band activity of about 43 Hz.

Criterion: the frequency of the largest peak of the Welch spectrum (1 s segments) in W of the PT5B SCH (2 ms bins), searched above 0 Hz and above 5 Hz; the LFP is a variant. The claims file's electrode readings are E1 (electrode 0) and E2 (mean of 11 electrodes); the files hold one trace, "LFP 0", taken here as E1, and E2 cannot be computed.

    row = {"claim": ID[c], "condition": m.CONDITIONS[c], "expected": f"{EXP_PEAK[c][0]} +/- {EXP_PEAK[c][1]}"}
    for lo in (0, 5):
        pk, f, p = m.welch_peak(cnt, 1 / m.SCH_BIN, lo)
        row[f"SCH peak >{lo} Hz"] = pk
        row[f"SCH ok >{lo}"] = within(pk, EXP_PEAK[c])
        SPEC[c] = (f, p)

    top = sorted(loc, key=lambda i: -pi[i])[:3]
    row["SCH top local maxima Hz (power ratio to largest)"] = [(float(fi[i]), round(float(pi[i] / pi[top[0]]), 2)) for i in top]
    rows.append(row)

Result: reproduced. The largest peak of the control rest PT5B SCH spectrum is at 19 Hz searched above 0 Hz and above 5 Hz, within 18 to 22 Hz. The LFP variant peaks at 1 Hz above 0 Hz and at 19 Hz above 5 Hz.

Result: reproduced. The control activated PT5B SCH spectrum peaks at 44 Hz under both search ranges, within 39.6 to 48.4 Hz. The LFP variant peaks at 1 Hz and 13 Hz.

Result: reproduced. The parkinsonian rest PT5B SCH spectrum peaks at 15 Hz under both search ranges, within 13.5 to 16.5 Hz; the LFP variant also peaks at 15 Hz.

Result: not reproduced. The parkinsonian activated PT5B SCH spectrum peaks at 27 Hz under both search ranges, outside 38.7 to 47.3 Hz; its next local maxima are at 30 and 21 Hz. The LFP variant also peaks at 27 Hz.

fig2c-control-pt5b-rate-activated¶

In the control condition PT5B neurons fire more in the activated state than at rest (11.7 +/- 9.4 against 26.8 +/- 18.2 spikes/s, p < 0.001).

Criterion: files -01 and -03, R1, R2 and R3; reproduced when under one rate reading all four values are within tolerance and the activated rates are higher with p < 0.001 under every test reading.

Result: partially reproduced (under R3, pairing the cells kept in both files). Under R3, IT2 rates are 1.203 +/- 1.649 spikes/s at rest and 6.662 +/- 8.858 activated, all four within tolerance, and the unpaired tests find the increase at p below 0.001 (Mann-Whitney 3.5e-05, Welch 3.6e-06). On the 25 cells kept in both files, the pairing adopted for pd-it6-rate-unchanged and fig5c-pd-it23-rate-activated, the paired tests find it at 0.016 (Wilcoxon) and 0.011 (paired t). So every test finds the increase, and two of four miss the criterion's p < 0.001. That is the pattern graded partially reproduced for activated-pt5b-rate-pd-vs-control, though weaker here: two tests miss the bound, not one, and the paired p-values come from 25 cells. On the 180 cells kept in either file, with 0 where a cell is absent, the paired tests give 0.69 (Wilcoxon) and 0.0013 (paired t), so the outcome rests on the pairing as well as on R3. The outcome was not reproduced until the third verification round, which agreed with the change. Under R1 (0.095 +/- 0.565 and 0.262 +/- 2.172) and R2 (1.555 +/- 1.723 and 8.883 +/- 9.220) the values are outside tolerance.

control-it5-silenced-activated¶

In the control condition IT5A and IT5B neurons fire at about 3 spikes/s at rest (3.3 and 3.1 spikes/s) and stop firing (0 spikes/s) in the activated state.

Criterion: files -01 and -03, readings R1 and R3; R2 a variant where defined. Tolerance 0.05 spikes/s for the zero rates.

In [16]:
def it5(cid, rest, act, exp):
    EXP[cid] = exp
    t = pd.concat([rate_rows("IT5A", [rest, act]), rate_rows("IT5B", [rest, act])])
    print(t.round(3).to_string(index=False))
    for reading in ["R1", "R1 (smallest block)", "R2", "R3"]:
        s = t[t.reading == reading].set_index(["pop", "file"])["mean"]
        vals = [s[("IT5A", rest)], s[("IT5B", rest)], s[("IT5A", act)], s[("IT5B", act)]]
        ok = [bool(within(v, e)) if np.isfinite(v) else False for v, e in zip(vals, exp)]
        print(f"{reading:22s} values {np.round(vals, 3).tolist()} expected {[e[0] for e in exp]} within {ok} all: {all(ok)}")
    for c in (act,):
        for p in ("IT5A", "IT5B"):
            n = sum(1 for g, q in D[c]["pop"].items() if q == p)
            sp = sum(len(t) for g, t in D[c]["trains"].items() if D[c]["pop"][g] == p)
            last = max((t[-1] for g, t in D[c]["trains"].items() if D[c]["pop"][g] == p), default=np.nan)
            print(f"{m.CONDITIONS[c]}: {p} units in the file {n}, spikes in 0-4.3 s {sp}, last spike at {last:.3f} s")

control-cv-isi and pd-cv-isi¶

control-cv-isi: In the control condition PT5B interspike-interval CV is highly variable at rest (0.59 +/- 0.37; 47.8% regular with CV <= 0.5, 52.2% irregular) and mainly irregular in the activated state (0.61 +/- 0.30; 25.7% regular, 74.3% irregular).

pd-cv-isi: In the parkinsonian condition PT5B spiking is mainly regular at rest (CV 0.34 +/- 0.27; 80.6% with CV <= 0.5) and more regular in the activated state (CV 0.18 +/- 0.19; 93.8% regular).

Criterion: CV of each PT5B cell's ISIs; mean and standard deviation over cells, share with CV <= 0.5; readings window (a) W or (b) 0 to 4.3 s, cells (i) with at least two ISIs or (ii) at least one. The ISI-CV statistic of NetPyNE 1.0.5 (plotSpikeStats, cells with more than 10 spikes in the time range) is shown as a variant (iii).

In [19]:
EXP["control-cv-isi"] = [(0.59, 0.059), (0.37, 0.037), (47.8, 4.78), (0.61, 0.061), (0.30, 0.030), (25.7, 2.57)]
EXP["pd-cv-isi"] = [(0.34, 0.034), (0.27, 0.027), (80.6, 8.06), (0.18, 0.018), (0.19, 0.019), (93.8, 9.38)]
CV = {}
for cid, (rest, act) in {"control-cv-isi": ("01", "03"), "pd-cv-isi": ("02", "04")}.items():
    print(cid)
    for wname, w in [("(a) W", m.WINDOW), ("(b) 0-4.3 s", (0.0, 4.3))]:
        for cname, k in [("(i) >=2 ISIs", 2), ("(ii) >=1 ISI", 1), ("(iii) >10 spikes, variant", 10)]:
            vals = []
            for c in (rest, act):
                pt = [t[(t >= w[0]) & (t < w[1])] for g, t in D[c]["trains"].items() if D[c]["pop"][g] == "PT5B"]
                cv = m.cv_isi(pt, k)
                vals += [cv.mean(), cv.std(ddof=1), 100 * np.mean(cv <= 0.5)]
                n = len(cv)
            ok = [bool(within(v, e)) for v, e in zip(vals, EXP[cid])]
            CV[(cid, wname, cname)] = vals
            print(f"  {wname:12s} {cname:26s} {np.round(vals, 3).tolist()}  within {ok} all: {all(ok)}  (n cells activated {n})")
    print("  expected", [e[0] for e in EXP[cid]])

control-subthreshold-oscillations and pd-no-subthreshold-oscillations (blocked)¶

control-subthreshold-oscillations: In the control condition subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations appear in 57.4% of PT5B neurons in the activated state and not at rest.

pd-no-subthreshold-oscillations: No subthreshold membrane-potential oscillations are seen in PT5B neurons in the parkinsonian rest or activated states.

The claims file finds no detection rule in the paper or its code and blocks both claims as methods_underspecified; it asks for the number of PT5B cells with a recorded potential.

pd-activated-vm-more-negative¶

In the activated state, PT5B membrane potential is on average more negative in the parkinsonian than in the control condition, which the paper gives as the reason the EPSPs look larger.

Criterion: files -03 and -04, the PT5B cells recorded in both, in W; readings (a) the mean of each trace and (b) its median; reproduced when the mean over cells is lower in the parkinsonian file under both.

control-duty-cycle and pd-duty-cycle¶

control-duty-cycle: In the control condition the PT5B duty cycle, the share of each oscillation period with activity above half-height, is 31% at rest and 48% in the activated state.

pd-duty-cycle: In the parkinsonian condition the PT5B duty cycle is 29% at rest and 25% in the activated state.

Criterion: PT5B SCH, 2 ms bins, unsmoothed; periods from one rising crossing of half-height to the next; readings half-height (a) halfway between the minimum and maximum of the window or (b) of each period; window (i) 2.0 to 2.25 s or (ii) W; summary (x) mean of per-period duty cycles or (y) total time above over total time of complete periods. Reproduced when under one combination both values of a claim are within tolerance.

LFP spectrograms: fig3a, fig3b, fig6a, fig6b¶

fig3a-control-rest-spectrogram: In the control rest state the LFP spectrogram shows virtually continuous power around 2 Hz and 15 to 25 Hz beta bursts recurring every 600 ms (1.7 Hz).

fig3b-control-activated-spectrogram: In the control activated state the 2 Hz activity disappears, 15 to 20 Hz power is no longer visible except 15 Hz bursts of about 100 to 500 ms at about 1.5 Hz, and brief (about 50 ms) 25 to 35 Hz bursts occur at about 1 Hz.

fig6a-pd-rest-spectrogram: In the parkinsonian rest state the LFP spectrogram shows continuous high-power 15 Hz beta with 25 to 35 Hz bursts of about 50 to 250 ms recurring about every 200 ms (about 5 Hz).

fig6b-pd-activated-spectrogram: In the parkinsonian activated state the LFP spectrogram shows 20 to 35 Hz bursts of about 25 to 100 ms recurring every 50 to 100 ms (about 10 to 20 Hz).

Readings S1 (NetPyNE 1.0.5 Morlet spectrogram, its defaults) and S2 (short-time Fourier transform), on "LFP 0" (E1; E2 cannot be computed). NetPyNE's own fft option with its defaults (256 samples at 40 kHz) has a frequency step of 156 Hz, printed below, so S2 uses a 250 ms Hann window with 90% overlap (4 Hz steps), a standard choice. That window has no bin between 1 and 3 Hz, so the 2 Hz test of S2 is also run with 1 s and 2 s windows. Burst rates are bursts per 2.3 s, the length of W. Bursts are epochs where the band's power is above halfway between its minimum and maximum in W (claims file). "Power around 2 Hz" is a local maximum of the time-averaged spectrum within 1 to 3 Hz.

In [23]:
import scipy.signal as sps
f_default = sps.spectrogram(np.zeros(92000), fs=m.FS, nperseg=256, noverlap=128, nfft=256)[0]
print("NetPyNE fft defaults: frequency step", f_default[1], "Hz; bins below 100 Hz:", f_default[f_default < 100].tolist())

TF = {}
for c, d in D.items():
    x = d["lfp"][int(2.0 * m.FS):int(4.3 * m.FS)]
    f1, t1, s1 = m.morlet_spec(x, m.FS)
    f2, t2, s2 = m.stft_spec(x, m.FS)
    TF[(c, "S1")] = (f1, t1, s1, 1 / m.FS)
    TF[(c, "S2")] = (f2, t2, s2, t2[1] - t2[0])

def low_max(f, S):
    """Frequencies in 1 to 3 Hz where the time-averaged spectrum has a local maximum."""
    tm = S.mean(axis=1)
    return [float(f[i]) for i in range(1, len(f) - 1) if tm[i] > tm[i - 1] and tm[i] > tm[i + 1] and 1 <= f[i] <= 3]

# A 250 ms window has 4 Hz steps and no bin between 1 and 3 Hz, so for the 2 Hz test S2 is also run
# with 1 s (1 Hz steps, 14 frames) and 2 s windows (0.5 Hz steps, 2 frames); bursts use 250 ms.
LOWMAX = {}
for c, d in D.items():
    x = d["lfp"][int(2.0 * m.FS):int(4.3 * m.FS)]
    for w in (1.0, 2.0):
        fw, tw, sw = m.stft_spec(x, m.FS, win_s=w)
        LOWMAX[(c, w)] = (low_max(fw, sw), len(tw))

def spec_row(c, s, bands):
    f, t, S, dt = TF[(c, s)]
    row = {"file": m.CONDITIONS[c], "reading": s, "local max 1-3 Hz": low_max(f, S),
           "mean 15-20 Hz power": m.band_power(f, S, (15, 20)).mean()}
    if s == "S2":
        row["local max 1-3 Hz, 1 s / 2 s windows"] = (LOWMAX[(c, 1.0)][0], LOWMAX[(c, 2.0)][0])
    for band in bands:
        b = m.band_bursts(t, m.band_power(f, S, band), dt, span=m.WINDOW[1] - m.WINDOW[0])
        row[f"{band} n"] = b["n"]
        row[f"{band} rate Hz"] = round(b["rate"], 2)
        row[f"{band} median ms"] = round(b["median_ms"], 1)
        row[f"{band} min-max ms"] = (round(b["durations"].min() * 1e3), round(b["durations"].max() * 1e3)) if b["n"] else None
        row[f"{band} frac above"] = round(b["frac_above"], 2)
    return row

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3))
for k, c in enumerate(D):
    f, t, S, dt = TF[(c, "S1")]
    ax[k].imshow(S[:, ::400], aspect="auto", origin="lower", extent=[2.0, 4.3, f[0], f[-1]], cmap="jet")
    ax[k].set_title(m.CONDITIONS[c] + " (S1)"); ax[k].set_xlabel("s"); ax[k].set_ylabel("Hz")
    print(m.CONDITIONS[c], "S1 plotted power range", S.min(), S.max())
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Result: not reproduced. Under S1 the time-averaged power has no local maximum within 1 to 3 Hz (it decreases from 1 Hz), and the 15 to 25 Hz burst rate is 1.30 Hz under S1 and 0.87 Hz under S2, outside 1.53 to 1.87 Hz. S2 with its 250 ms window has no bin between 1 and 3 Hz and so no maximum there; with 1 s and 2 s windows S2 has one (at 1 and 2 Hz), so the 2 Hz part holds under S2 with a long window. The outcome is the same under every reading, since S1 fails both parts and the burst rate fails under both.

Result: not reproduced. Two parts hold under both readings with their burst windows: no 1 to 3 Hz maximum, and 15 to 20 Hz power lower than at rest (ratio 0.42 under S1, 0.57 under S2). With a 1 s window S2 has a maximum at 1 Hz, and with a 2 s window none. The 14 to 16 Hz burst rate is 1.30 Hz (S1) and 2.61 Hz (S2) against 1.5 +/- 0.15, the 25 to 35 Hz burst rate 1.30 and 0.87 Hz against 1.0 +/- 0.1, its median duration 66.9 and 100 ms against 50 +/- 5, and the 14 to 16 Hz bursts last 155 to 557 ms under S1 and 50 to 300 ms under S2, each outside 90 to 550 ms at one end. Burst rates are bursts per 2.3 s under both readings.

control-coincident-spikes and pd-coincident-spikes¶

control-coincident-spikes: In the control condition 1% of PT5B spikes are coincident with another PT5B spike within 1 ms at rest, and 3% in the activated state.

pd-coincident-spikes: In the parkinsonian condition 2% of PT5B spikes are coincident (2 or more spikes in 1 ms) at rest and 3% in the activated state.

Readings (a) a spike of another PT5B cell within 1 ms either side or (b) in the same 1 ms bin; windows (i) W, (ii) 0.3 to 4.3 s, (iii) 0 to 4.0 s. Reproduced when under one combination both values are within tolerance. As a variant, not a reading of the claims file, the same share among the 20 PT5B cells whose potentials are recorded.

Result: not reproduced. Under every reading 99.99% to 100% of control PT5B spikes have a spike of another PT5B cell within 1 ms, against 1% and 3%: the 1,435 PT5B cells fire 17 to 42 spikes per ms together. Among only the 20 recorded cells the share is still 24.8% to 72.8%. The paper's 1% to 3% cannot come from all PT5B cells with this definition; whether the claims file reads the paper's measure correctly is asked of a reader (questions/001444.yaml).

Result: not reproduced. Under every reading 99.95% to 100% of parkinsonian PT5B spikes are coincident, against 2% and 3%; among the 20 recorded cells, 27.0% to 72.2%. The reading is asked of a reader, as for the control files.

Unitary events: fig4-control-unitary-events, fig7-pd-unitary-events, rest-synchrony-increase¶

fig4-control-unitary-events: In the control condition, PT5B coincident firing above that expected from rate-matched Poisson processes occurs at rest in 100 to 275 ms clusters with 15 to 24 Hz periodicity (mean 19 Hz), totalling 0.7 of 4.0 s (17.5%), and in the activated state in more frequent 125 to 250 ms clusters totalling 1.1 of 4.0 s (27.5%).

fig7-pd-unitary-events: In the parkinsonian condition, significant PT5B coincident firing occurs at rest in 400 to 1100 ms clusters of 6 to 16 periods at 14 to 15 Hz (mean 15 Hz), totalling 3.1 of 4.0 s (77.5%), and in the activated state in 100 to 350 ms epochs totalling 1.4 of 4.0 s (35.0%).

rest-synchrony-increase: At rest, PT5B spike synchrony is substantially larger in the parkinsonian than in the control condition (significant synchrony 3.1 against 0.7 of 4.0 s).

Method of the claims file: coincidences are 2 or more PT5B spikes within 1 ms; expected count from Poisson cells at their rates in the 100 ms window; a window is significant when the joint-surprise p < 0.05; significant periods are the union of significant windows. Readings: windows (a) slid in 1 ms steps or (b) non-overlapping; span (i) 0.3 to 4.3 s or (ii) 0 to 4.0 s; periodicity (x) SCH spectral peak or (y) inverse mean interval between SCH peaks.

The claims file does not say how a window's coincidences are counted, and the paper says only that it found "synchronous spikes significantly above the expected number of synchronous spikes for the neuron population size and firing rates" (Methods, Identifying synchronous spiking). Four counts are run (helper, unitary_events): (1) bins, the number of 1 ms bins where 2 or more PT5B cells fire, with a Poisson joint-surprise test; (2) spikes, the spikes in such bins; (3) pairs, the number of pairs of cells firing in the same bin (Grun's coincidence count summed over all pairs of PT5B cells), against independent cells at the window's rates; (4) the same pair count against a null that keeps each cell's number of active bins in the window and places them at random. Counts (3) and (4) take the normal tail with the exact mean and variance of their null. The chance level of each is measured first, on independent Poisson cells.

In [29]:
# Chance level and sensitivity of the four counts on synthetic spike trains (seeded): (1) 1,435
# independent Poisson cells at 15 and 30 spikes/s, the PT5B population at rest and activated, so
# every significant window is a false positive; (2) 100 cells at 10 spikes/s with 20 pair
# coincidences added in 1.0 to 1.1 s; (3) 20 cells at 2 spikes/s all firing together 11 times.
rng_ue = np.random.default_rng(1444)
COUNTS = ["bins", "spikes", "pairs (rate null)", "pairs (count null)"]
def poisson_pop(n, rate, span=(0.3, 4.3)):
    return {"trains": {g: np.sort(rng_ue.uniform(*span, rng_ue.poisson(rate * (span[1] - span[0])))) for g in range(n)},
            "pop": {g: "X" for g in range(n)}}
rows = []
for rate in (15, 30):
    null = poisson_pop(1435, rate)
    for cnt in COUNTS:
        for sname, step in [("(a) 1 ms steps", 0.001), ("(b) non-overlapping", 0.1)]:
            u = m.unitary_events(null, "X", (0.3, 4.3), step, count=cnt)
            rows.append({"case": f"null, 1435 cells at {rate}/s", "count": cnt, "windows": sname,
                         "significant windows": f"{u['n_sig_windows']}/{u['n_windows']}", "significant s": round(u["total_s"], 3)})
inj = poisson_pop(100, 10)
for e in rng_ue.uniform(1.0, 1.1, 20):
    a_, b_ = rng_ue.choice(100, 2, replace=False)
    inj["trains"][a_] = np.sort(np.r_[inj["trains"][a_], e]); inj["trains"][b_] = np.sort(np.r_[inj["trains"][b_], e + 0.0002])
syn = poisson_pop(20, 2)
ev = rng_ue.uniform(0.5, 4.2, 11)
for g in syn["trains"]:
    syn["trains"][g] = np.sort(np.r_[syn["trains"][g], ev])
for name, d_, truth in [("100 cells, 20 pairs added in 1.0-1.1 s", inj, "window 1.0-1.1 s"),
                        ("20 cells firing together 11 times", syn, f"{len(set(np.floor((ev - 0.3) / 0.1).astype(int)))} windows hold an event")]:
    for cnt in COUNTS:
        u = m.unitary_events(d_, "X", (0.3, 4.3), 0.1, count=cnt)
        rows.append({"case": name, "count": cnt, "windows": "(b) non-overlapping",
                     "significant windows": f"{u['n_sig_windows']}/{u['n_windows']}",
                     "significant s": round(u["total_s"], 3), "where": [round(0.3 + 0.1 * j, 1) for j in range(40) if u["sig"][j * 100]], "truth": truth})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

    print("  any combination meets the criterion:", any(v for k_, v in UEOK.items() if k_[0] == cid))

Result: not reproduced. No combination of count, window placement, span and periodicity reading meets the criterion. Counting coincident bins or the spikes in them, no window is significant (0 of 3,901 slid and 0 of 40 non-overlapping windows), since two or more PT5B cells fire in every 1 ms bin of 0.3 to 4.3 s and the bin count is at its maximum of 100 in 92% to 100% of control windows; these counts cannot exceed their expectation. Counting pairs of cells against independent cells at the window's rates, the significant duration is 0.8 to 1.65 s at rest against 0.63 to 0.77 s, and 1.0 to 1.43 s activated, within 0.99 to 1.21 s for two of four combinations; rest clusters last up to 552 ms, outside 90 to 302.5 ms, and the activated state does not have more significant periods. The periodicity reading (x) gives 18.0 to 19.8 Hz at rest, within 17.1 to 20.9 Hz. On independent Poisson cells this count finds no significant window, and it misses 20 added pair coincidences, so it is conservative. Counting pairs against a null that keeps each cell's active bins, 3.2 to 3.99 s are significant at rest and 3.7 to 3.99 s activated; on independent cells this count finds 1 or 2 of 40 windows, but its slid windows cover 0.64 to 0.75 s by chance alone.

Result: not reproduced. No combination meets the criterion. Counting bins or spikes, no window is significant (0 s against 3.1 and 1.4 s), with two or more PT5B cells firing in 99.1% (rest) and 100% (activated) of 1 ms bins. Counting pairs against independent cells, 3.8 to 3.98 s are significant at rest against 2.79 to 3.41 s, in two clusters of 1,500 to 2,379 ms (outside 360 to 1,210 ms), and 0 to 0.43 s activated against 1.26 to 1.54 s; reading (x) gives a rest periodicity of 15.1 to 15.4 Hz, within 13.5 to 16.5 Hz. Against the null that keeps each cell's active bins, all 4.0 s at rest and 3.7 to 4.0 s activated are significant.

rest-synchrony-increase¶

Reproduced when the total duration of significant synchrony at rest is larger in the parkinsonian file under every reading.

In [31]:
for cnt in COUNTS:
    for sname in ["(a) 1 ms steps", "(b) non-overlapping"]:
        for spname in ["(i) 0.3-4.3 s", "(ii) 0-4.0 s"]:
            a, b = UE[("01", cnt, sname, spname)][0]["total_s"], UE[("02", cnt, sname, spname)][0]["total_s"]
            print(f"{cnt:18s} {sname:20s} {spname:14s} control {a:.3f} s, parkinsonian {b:.3f} s, parkinsonian larger: {b > a}")
# Both pair nulls take each cell's spikes as spread evenly over its 100 ms window, so the excess also
# tracks how strongly the population rhythm modulates firing within a window.
print("\nMedian observed / expected per window at rest, (a)(i), (a)(ii), (b)(i), (b)(ii):")
for cnt in ["pairs (rate null)", "pairs (count null)"]:
    print(" ", cnt, {m.CONDITIONS[c]: [round(float(np.median(UE[(c, cnt, s, sp)][0]["obs"] / UE[(c, cnt, s, sp)][0]["exp"])), 3)
                                    for s in ["(a) 1 ms steps", "(b) non-overlapping"] for sp in ["(i) 0.3-4.3 s", "(ii) 0-4.0 s"]] for c in ("01", "02")})
(f1, p1), (f2, p2) = SPEC["01"], SPEC["02"]
sel = (f1 > 5) & (f1 <= 100)
print("Largest PT5B SCH spectral power above 5 Hz in W: control rest", f"{p1[sel].max():.3g}", "parkinsonian rest", f"{p2[sel].max():.3g}",
      "ratio", round(float(p2[sel].max() / p1[sel].max()), 1))

Largest PT5B SCH spectral power above 5 Hz in W: control rest 12.3 parkinsonian rest 387 ratio 31.5

Result: reproduced, under the pair count. Counting coincident bins or spikes, the significant synchrony at rest is 0 s in both files under every reading, but those counts are at their ceiling in every file and cannot find synchrony at all (the bin count also misses both synthetic cases above). Counting pairs of coincident cells, the one count that can exceed its expectation here, the parkinsonian rest file has more significant synchrony under every window reading: 3.8 to 3.98 s against 0.8 to 1.65 s against independent cells, and 4.0 s against 3.2 to 3.99 s against the null that keeps each cell's active bins. The outcome rests on the pair count as an assumption, with two caveats. Under the count-preserving null the comparison is at its ceiling (4.0 against 3.98 and 3.99 s for slid windows), and on independent cells that null's slid windows already cover 0.64 to 0.75 s by chance, so the comparison rests in effect on the rate null, which is conservative. Both pair nulls take each cell's spikes as spread evenly over its 100 ms window, so the excess partly measures how strongly the population rhythm modulates firing within a window: the median observed over expected pair count is higher at parkinsonian rest than at control rest (printed above), and the largest PT5B SCH spectral power is many times higher (ratio printed above). The paper's own Poisson window null probably shares this property.

Result: not reproduced. Under R3 parkinsonian IT2 rates are 0.783 +/- 1.105 at rest and 4.295 +/- 7.066 activated, all four within tolerance, and the Welch test finds the increase at p = 1.7e-04. The Mann-Whitney test gives 0.0018, above 0.001. On the 22 cells kept in both files the paired tests give 0.60 (Wilcoxon) and 0.21 (paired t), and on the 99 cells kept in either file 2.4e-04 and 2.2e-04. Under neither pairing do all four tests reach p < 0.001. The pairings grade differently: with the cells kept in both files the paired tests find no increase, while with the cells kept in either every test finds the increase at p < 0.01 and only Mann-Whitney misses 0.001, the pattern graded partially reproduced for activated-pt5b-rate-pd-vs-control. The outcome rests on pairing the cells kept in both files, the choice adopted for pd-it6-rate-unchanged. Under R1 (0.025 +/- 0.239 and 0.164 +/- 1.598) and R2 (1.163 +/- 1.173 and 6.163 +/- 7.769) the values are outside tolerance.

rest-beta-power-order-of-magnitude¶

At rest, LFP beta power around 15 Hz is an order of magnitude larger in the parkinsonian than in the control condition.

Criterion: files -01 and -02, LFP in W, readings S1, S2 (E1 only); power (a) at 15 Hz and (b) mean over 14 to 16 Hz; ratio of time-averaged parkinsonian to control power; reproduced when the ratio is in 3.16 to 31.6 under every reading, not reproduced when below 3.16 under every reading. As a variant, the ratio of the spectrograms' maxima (the colour bars of Figs. 3 and 6 are x 10^-5 and x 10^-4).

In [41]:
rows = []
for s in ("S1", "S2"):
    f1, _, S1c, _ = TF[("01", s)]
    f2, _, S2p, _ = TF[("02", s)]
    at15 = lambda f, S: S[np.argmin(np.abs(f - 15))].mean()
    for name, fn in [("(a) at 15 Hz", at15), ("(b) 14-16 Hz", lambda f, S: m.band_power(f, S, (14, 16)).mean())]:
        a, b = fn(f1, S1c), fn(f2, S2p)
        rows.append({"reading": s, "measure": name, "control": a, "parkinsonian": b, "ratio": b / a,

    rows.append({"reading": s, "measure": "variant, max over the spectrogram", "control": S1c.max(), "parkinsonian": S2p.max(),
                 "ratio": S2p.max() / S1c.max(), "log10 ratio": np.log10(S2p.max() / S1c.max()),

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The files hold one LFP trace, so only electrode reading E1 was run, taking "LFP 0" as electrode 0; E2 (mean of 11 electrodes) could not be. The spectrogram reading S2 uses a 250 ms window, since NetPyNE's own fft defaults cannot resolve below 156 Hz. Population sizes for R1 come from the gid blocks, since silent cells are not stored. The paper's IT rates match exactly when the mean is taken over the cells that fired at any time in the simulation (R3, the cells the file holds), and not over all cells (R1) or the cells active in W (R2). R3 was added to the claims file's readings in answer to a question; the paper does not say which cells enter a mean, so the eight IT outcomes that hold only under R3 rest on it as an assumption. Under R2 and R3 the paired tests were run on the cells kept in both files and on those kept in either (at 0 where absent); the first pairing is adopted, and pd-it6-rate-unchanged, fig2c-control-it23-rate-activated and fig5c-pd-it23-rate-activated rest on it. The coincidence and unitary-event analyses follow the claims file's definitions over all PT5B cells. With 17 to 42 PT5B spikes per ms, the share of coincident spikes and the counts of coincident bins or spikes saturate; the paper must have used another set of cells or another measure for its 1% to 3%, which it does not state, and a reader is asked. For the unitary events, pairs of coincident cells were also counted, against two nulls, and rest-synchrony-increase rests on that count. The S2 spectrogram's 2 Hz test was also run with 1 s and 2 s windows; no outcome changes.

What was found about the dataset. The units table holds only the cells that fired (2,917 to 4,480 of 10,073 M1 cells in the paper's set), where the description says spike trains of all 10,073 neurons. The paper's set holds 20 PT5B potentials per file, not 400, and those potentials match their cells' stored spikes only in the first half second; in W they seem to come from a run that diverged from the stored spikes, which the files cannot establish. sub-001/sub-001.nwb duplicates sub-001_ses-sM1-04-22-2024-01.nwb. Each file holds one LFP trace with no electrode position. The files' related publication is the preprint, the dandiset lists no related resource, and its summary names spike sorting as the technique of a simulation.
